intro: Field Trip Health Kitchener-Waterloo is an outpatient clinic at 180 Columbia Street West in Waterloo, a short walk from the University of Waterloo. Adults from Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge and Guelph come here for ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, mostly for depression, anxiety, PTSD and OCD that earlier treatment hasn't eased enough.

Nobody stays overnight. You book a dosing session on a weekday, spend about two and a half hours in a private room with a therapist, then someone drives you home. The clinic is one of eight Canadian locations run under the Field Trip Health Canada name, and it keeps its own Waterloo team of social workers, psychotherapists and nurses.

pillars.title: Medicine and therapy in the same room
pillars.body: A dosing session in Waterloo lasts about two and a half hours. A nurse gives a low dose of ketamine, usually as an injection, and a therapist stays with you while it takes effect. You lie back in a zero-gravity chair under a weighted blanket, with noise-cancelling headphones and a playlist, and the therapist helps you make sense of the experience afterwards. Most plans run 6 or 9 of these sessions, with integration appointments in between.

pillars.title: A basement clinic on Columbia Street West
pillars.body: The clinic is in Suite B1 of 180 Columbia Street West, on the lower level. Take the elevator down and follow the signs to the door. Parking on site is free, but plan for someone else to drive you home after a dosing day. By transit it is about a 10-minute walk from University of Waterloo station on the ION line, and Grand River Transit buses stop nearby. From Kitchener GO station it is a short bus ride.

pillars.title: A local team of social workers and psychotherapists
pillars.body: The therapy side in Waterloo is run by registered social workers and registered psychotherapists, including Vanessa Bauer, who has more than ten years in mental health and addictions work, and River Page, a registered psychotherapist who works with trauma, anxiety and relationship problems. A nurse clinic manager, practical nurses and a group of nurse practitioners handle the medical side, under physician Dr. Mario Nucci.

overviewH2: How care works at the Waterloo clinic
overview: Before anyone is offered medicine, there is a screening process. It starts with a free 15-minute discovery call, then a paid 50-minute consultation with a nurse practitioner, which OHIP does not cover. The nurse practitioner goes through your physical and mental health history and decides whether this treatment is safe for you. Pregnancy, a history of psychosis or schizophrenia, uncontrolled high blood pressure and a recent serious head injury can all rule it out.

If you are a good fit, you choose a 6 or 9 session plan. Each dosing session is supervised, and the medicine is usually given by intramuscular injection, though nasal or under-the-tongue doses are possible. Your therapist meets you before the first session to set goals and again afterwards to talk through what came up, which the clinic calls integration.

afterOverview: The Waterloo therapy team is mostly registered social workers and registered psychotherapists, and several of them also see clients for ordinary talk therapy, in person or online. The clinic also offers pain management and stellate ganglion block, an injection some people with PTSD ask about. It does not offer MDMA or psilocybin therapy, because neither is approved for routine clinical use in Canada, and it makes no promise about results.

faqIntro: Answers come from the Kitchener-Waterloo clinic's own page. Still unsure? Call, it's free and confidential.

faqs.q: Is Field Trip Health Kitchener-Waterloo a residential rehab?
faqs.a: No. It is an outpatient clinic in Waterloo that runs weekday appointments, and you go home after each visit. There are no beds and no detox. If you need live-in treatment or supervised withdrawal, ask about it on the discovery call or compare residential centres elsewhere in Ontario.

faqs.q: What does the Waterloo clinic treat?
faqs.a: The clinic uses ketamine-assisted psychotherapy mainly for depression, anxiety, PTSD, OCD, substance use and chronic pain, usually after other treatments have not helped enough. Its therapists also see people for grief, ADHD, eating disorders, bipolar disorder, postpartum depression and trauma, including PTSD in veterans and first responders. Results differ from person to person.

faqs.q: How much does it cost, and can I use my benefits?
faqs.a: Field Trip Health does not publish prices; cost depends on how the medicine is given and how many sessions your plan includes, and the team explains it on the free discovery call. The nurse practitioner consultation has a fee because OHIP does not cover it. Public plans do not pay for the medical part, but many people claim the psychotherapy or nursing portion through extended health benefits, and third-party financing is available.

faqs.q: How long is each session, and how many will I need?
faqs.a: A dosing session in Waterloo takes about 2.5 hours, including preparation, the medicine itself and a first integration talk. Field Trip's standard plans have 6 or 9 dosing sessions. After the core sessions you meet the team again to decide whether more care makes sense.

faqs.q: Who can be treated, and do I need a referral?
faqs.a: Anyone can book the free discovery call without a referral, and doctors can also refer through the clinic's referral form or Ocean eReferral. Eligibility is always decided by a nurse practitioner. The treatment may not suit people who are pregnant, have a history of psychosis or schizophrenia, have uncontrolled high blood pressure, a recent serious head injury or an allergy to the medicine.

faqs.q: Where is the clinic and how do I get there?
faqs.a: It is at 180 Columbia Street West, Unit B1, in Waterloo, on the lower level of the building. Take the elevator to the basement and follow the signs. University of Waterloo ION station is about a 10-minute walk away, Grand River Transit buses stop nearby, and a short bus ride connects from Kitchener GO station. Parking is free on site.

faqs.q: Can I drive home after a session?
faqs.a: No. You may feel drowsy after the medicine, so the clinic asks you to arrange a ride home on every dosing day. It also asks you to skip alcohol and recreational drugs beforehand and to avoid a heavy meal.

faqs.q: Is the Waterloo clinic wheelchair accessible?
faqs.a: Yes. The clinic says it is wheelchair accessible, with elevator access to the lower level, and service animals are welcome.

faqs.q: Does Field Trip Health Kitchener-Waterloo offer MDMA or psilocybin therapy?
faqs.a: No. Those substances are still controlled in Canada and are not approved for routine clinical use, so the clinic only offers the one psychedelic medicine that a physician can legally prescribe here. It is given mainly by intramuscular injection, sometimes by nasal spray or under the tongue.

The clinic operates under the Field Trip Health Canada name, with locations in Waterloo, Toronto, Hamilton, Ottawa, Thunder Bay, Sault Ste. Marie, Vancouver and Montreal. After the original company's 2023 restructuring, its Canadian clinics passed to the Canadian Centre for Psychedelic Healing. The US clinics are a separate business now, so use fieldtriphealth.ca for Waterloo.
